words.etymology: From Latin bene, meaning well, and volens, meaning wishing.

senses.definition: kind and generous towards other people, especially those with less power
wishing to do good rather than to gain something

examples.sentence: A benevolent stranger paid for the whole table and left before anyone could thank him.
The fund depends on one benevolent donor who prefers to stay unknown.

words.etymology: From Latin male, meaning badly, and volens, meaning wishing.

senses.definition: wishing harm on other people, and pleased when harm arrives

examples.sentence: There was something malevolent in the way he smiled at the bad news.

words.etymology: From Latin ambi, meaning both, and valens, meaning strong.

senses.definition: having two opposite feelings about something at the same time

examples.sentence: She was ambivalent about the offer: better pay, but a city she disliked.

words.etymology: From Latin benignus, meaning well born and so kindly.

senses.definition: gentle and causing no harm at all
of an illness, not dangerous and not spreading

examples.sentence: The old dog gave the children a benign look and went back to sleep.

words.etymology: From Latin malignus, meaning of a bad nature.

senses.definition: to say unfair and harmful things about a person
having a harmful effect that spreads quietly

examples.sentence: It is easy to malign a plan you never had to build yourself.

words.etymology: From Latin bene, meaning well, and facere, meaning to do.

senses.definition: a person who gives money or help to a person or a cause

examples.sentence: The library was built by a benefactor whose name nobody wrote down.

words.etymology: From Latin beneficium, meaning a favour or a service done.

senses.definition: a person who receives money or help from somebody else

examples.sentence: Every beneficiary of the fund had to be named in the letter.

words.etymology: From Latin voluntas, meaning will or choice.

senses.definition: done because you choose to, not because you are made to

examples.sentence: Attendance is voluntary, but almost everyone comes anyway.

words.etymology: From Latin volo, meaning I wish.

senses.definition: the power to choose what you do, and the act of choosing it

examples.sentence: He left of his own volition, with no one asking him to go.

words.etymology: From Latin scrutari, meaning to search even through the rubbish.

senses.definition: to look at something very closely and for a long time

examples.sentence: The committee will scrutinize every claim before it signs anything.

words.etymology: From the same Latin root as scrutinize, meaning a close search.

senses.definition: careful and complete attention paid to something

examples.sentence: The plan fell apart under scrutiny, which is what scrutiny is for.

words.etymology: From Latin meticulosus, meaning fearful, later careful.

senses.definition: showing great care about small details

examples.sentence: Her notes were meticulous: every date, every name, every page.

words.etymology: From Latin diligere, meaning to value and so to attend to.

senses.definition: working with steady care and effort

examples.sentence: A diligent student is not always the fastest one in the room.

words.etymology: From Latin neglegere, meaning to not pick up, to ignore.

senses.definition: failing to give the care that a duty requires

examples.sentence: The report found the office negligent, not dishonest.

words.etymology: From Latin vigilare, meaning to stay awake.

senses.definition: watching carefully for danger or trouble

examples.sentence: Stay vigilant on the last mile, when everyone stops looking.

words.etymology: From Latin providens, meaning seeing ahead.

senses.definition: careful to avoid trouble that can be seen coming

examples.sentence: It was prudent to keep a second copy of the file.

words.etymology: The Latin prefix im, meaning not, joined to prudent.

senses.definition: not thinking about what will follow; unwise

examples.sentence: Spending the whole budget in one week was imprudent.

words.etymology: From Greek meta, meaning change, and morphe, meaning form.

senses.definition: a complete change of form, as when an insect becomes an adult

examples.sentence: The metamorphosis takes days, and nothing of the old shape is kept.

words.etymology: From Latin transire, meaning to go across and pass on.

senses.definition: lasting only a short time and then gone

examples.sentence: The pain was transient, but the lesson was not.

words.etymology: From Latin mitis, meaning soft, and agere, meaning to make.

senses.definition: to make something bad less serious

examples.sentence: Nothing can undo the storm; the plan can only mitigate the damage.

words.etymology: From Latin levis, meaning light, so to make lighter.

senses.definition: to make pain or a problem easier to bear

examples.sentence: Warm water will alleviate the ache, though it will not cure it.

words.etymology: From Latin acerbus, meaning bitter, so to make more bitter.

senses.definition: to make a bad situation worse

examples.sentence: Arguing about who is at fault will only exacerbate the delay.

words.etymology: From Latin resilire, meaning to jump back.

senses.definition: able to return to normal quickly after harm or trouble

examples.sentence: Small teams can be surprisingly resilient when the money runs out.

words.etymology: From Latin tenere, meaning to hold.

senses.definition: holding on to something and refusing to let go

examples.sentence: She was tenacious about the one question everybody else had dropped.
